text: A route table is a set of rules deciding where traffic leaving a subnet goes next — each route is just a destination CIDR plus a target. Every VPC gets a main route table automatically, and any subnet you don't explicitly associate elsewhere uses it. Real designs usually create a custom table per subnet tier instead and associate each subnet with it explicitly — one table per subnet at a time, though one table can serve several subnets that should all route the same way.

Every route table, the moment it's created, already contains a local route for the VPC's own CIDR block, letting every subnet talk to every other subnet by default. You can't edit or delete that one — everything you add afterward, like a route to an Internet Gateway, a NAT Gateway, or a peering connection, simply sits alongside it, never replacing it.

A private subnet with zero internet routes at all is often too strict in practice — it still needs to pull OS patches or call an external API, even though nothing on the internet should ever reach it directly. A NAT Gateway solves exactly that: it lets instances start outbound connections to the internet while staying completely unreachable from the internet side, because it only forwards traffic that's a response to something the private instance started first.

A NAT Gateway is AWS-managed, needs its own Elastic IP, and has to live in a public subnet — not the private one it actually serves. Once it exists, the private subnet's route table picks up a 0.0.0.0/0 route pointing at the NAT Gateway's ID, sitting right alongside that untouchable local route for the VPC's own CIDR block.

Compare that table to a public subnet's from Lesson 14: same local route, same 0.0.0.0/0 destination, but the target is an Internet Gateway instead of a NAT Gateway. One target is the entire line between a subnet that's reachable from the internet and one that can only reach out to it. Next, Lesson 16 covers the two firewalls that actually decide what traffic gets this far in the first place.
